blocks.content: Picture two different interviews. In the first, the interviewer says design a link shortener for a small internal team of 200 people. In the second, they say design one for the entire internet, billions of clicks a month. If you sketch the same architecture for both, you have already lost the round before you drew a single box.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382290-166174939.png
blocks.alt: A small scale system, hundred users a day, served fine by one server and one database

blocks.content: The difference between those two systems is not cleverness. It is scale. A single server next to a database is a perfectly good answer for the first case and a disaster waiting to happen for the second.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382290-449355514.png
blocks.alt: A huge scale system needing a load balancer, many app servers, and a sharded database with a cache

blocks.content: Capacity estimation is the skill of figuring out that scale before you design anything at all. People often call it back of the envelope math, because that is exactly what it looks like, quick multiplication on paper, not a spreadsheet.
1. Introduction

Almost every solid system design interview starts with a few rough numbers. How many users. How many requests a second. How much data gets stored. Interviewers ask for these because the right architecture depends entirely on them.

A design that works fine for 100 users a day and a design that survives 100 million users a day look nothing alike. One is a single server with a database sitting next to it. The other needs load balancers, caching layers, sharded storage, and probably a CDN.

If you skip estimation, you will spend the first ten minutes designing for the wrong scale, then have to backtrack the moment the interviewer mentions the real numbers. That backtracking costs you far more time than doing the estimate up front ever would.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Estimating scale early is not busywork, it decides whether you reach for a single database or a fleet of shards, whether a cache is even necessary, and whether one region is enough. Skip it, and you might spend the next thirty minutes designing the wrong thing entirely.
The good news is that none of this requires you to be a math whiz. It requires you to be comfortable multiplying round numbers and comfortable saying your assumptions out loud.
2. Roughly Right, Not Precisely Correct
This is the part that trips people up. The interviewer does not want an exact number. They want to see you reason in orders of magnitude.

If you estimate 8,000 requests a second and the real figure turns out to be 10,000, that is fine, you were roughly right and the architecture barely changes. But if you estimate 8,000 and the real figure is 800,000, that is a different problem altogether. Being off by 20 percent is a rounding error. Being off by 100x means you designed the wrong system.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382290-871063415.png
blocks.alt: Being off by 20 percent still leaves a useful estimate, while being off by 100x leads to designing the wrong system entirely

blocks.title: Round aggressively
blocks.content: Round 86,400 seconds in a day to 100,000. Round 365 days to 400. Round a million to 10 to the 6th power and just keep the exponent. None of this meaningfully changes the architecture decision, and it saves you from doing ugly arithmetic live in front of someone.
3. The Building Blocks of an Estimate
blocks.text: 3. The Building Blocks of an Estimate

blocks.content: Almost every capacity estimate is built from the same handful of ingredients. Learn the pattern once, and you can apply it to whatever system the interviewer throws at you next.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382291-820061861.png
blocks.alt: Daily active users flowing into requests per second, flowing into storage growth, flowing into bandwidth

blocks.content: ["Daily active users, the starting point for everything else","Requests per second, derived from users and their average actions per day","Read QPS versus write QPS, since the two put very different load on a system","Storage growth per day and per year, from average item size times item count","Bandwidth, from QPS times average payload size"]
items: Daily active users, the starting point for everything else
Requests per second, derived from users and their average actions per day
Read QPS versus write QPS, since the two put very different load on a system
Storage growth per day and per year, from average item size times item count
Bandwidth, from QPS times average payload size

blocks.content: 3.1 Daily Active Users

Everything starts here. DAU is how many distinct users actually use the product on a given day. The interviewer will usually just hand you this number, something like 10 million DAU for a mid size app, or 200 million for something Twitter sized.
If they do not give it to you, ask. Guessing a user base out of thin air is one of the few places where being wrong by 100x happens by accident rather than by a reasonable rounding choice.
3.2 Requests Per Second, From DAU to QPS
blocks.text: 3.2 Requests Per Second, From DAU to QPS

blocks.content: Once you know DAU, you need how many actions each user performs a day. For a search engine that might be 10 searches a day. For a chat app it might be 40 messages. Multiply DAU by actions per user and you get a total daily action count.
QPS = (DAU x actions per user per day) / 86400 seconds

code.content: QPS = (DAU x actions per user per day) / 86400 seconds

codes.text: QPS = (DAU x actions per user per day) / 86400 seconds

blocks.content: Divide that daily total by the number of seconds in a day and you get average requests per second, the QPS number the interviewer actually cares about.
3.3 Read QPS Versus Write QPS
Not all requests are equal. Reading a post and writing a new one put very different load on your system, and almost every real product reads far more than it writes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382291-322440072.png
blocks.alt: Total QPS splitting into a heavier read QPS path and a lighter write QPS path

blocks.content: A common starting assumption is a 100 to 1 ratio of reads to writes for social and content apps. Chat and messaging systems tend to sit closer to 1 to 1, since every message sent is also a message read. State whichever ratio you are assuming out loud, then keep moving.
3.4 Storage Growth, Per Day and Per Year
blocks.text: 3.4 Storage Growth, Per Day and Per Year

blocks.content: Storage is just average item size times how many items get created a day. Do that once for a single day, then multiply by 365 for a rough yearly figure.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382292-508329392.png
blocks.alt: Storage from each day adding on top of the previous day, keeping the total growing over time

blocks.content: Storage estimates matter because they tell you roughly when a single database stops being enough, and roughly when you will need sharding, a cold storage tier, or object storage for large files like images and video.
3.5 Bandwidth, From QPS to Bytes Per Second
blocks.text: 3.5 Bandwidth, From QPS to Bytes Per Second

blocks.content: Bandwidth is what happens when you multiply QPS by average payload size. It tells you whether the network, not the CPU, ends up being your bottleneck.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382292-707844543.png
blocks.alt: QPS multiplied by average payload size producing a bandwidth figure

blocks.content: This one surprises people more than it should. A service can have plenty of spare CPU and still fall over because every single request drags along a fat payload.
4. Numbers Worth Having Ready
You do not need a memorized formula sheet. You need a couple of shortcuts you can derive in seconds, live, without reaching for a calculator.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383028-408488437.png
blocks.alt: A daily total of requests divided by 86400 seconds producing a rough average QPS

blocks.title: The 86,400 shortcut
blocks.text: There are 86,400 seconds in a day. Round that to 100,000. Now any daily total divided by 100,000 gives you a rough average QPS in your head. 50 million requests a day becomes about 500 QPS. No calculator needed.

blocks.content: Interviewers do not expect you to have 86,400 memorized down to the exact digit. They expect you to know it is roughly 100,000 and derive the rest fast, out loud, instead of disappearing into your own head for two minutes.

blocks.title: A few more numbers worth knowing
blocks.content: A million is 10 to the 6th. A billion is 10 to the 9th. A byte is 8 bits. A megabyte is roughly a million bytes, a gigabyte roughly a billion. None of these need to be exact, they need to be fast.
5. Peak Versus Average Load
Average QPS is a comforting number, and also a little bit of a lie. Real traffic is not spread evenly across the day, it clusters around certain hours.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383030-969345468.png
blocks.alt: Average QPS multiplied by a peak factor of 2x to 3x producing the actual peak QPS a system needs to survive

blocks.content: A common rule of thumb is that peak QPS runs about 2 to 3x average QPS. Lunchtime, evenings, and overlapping time zones all push traffic well above the daily average.

blocks.title: Design for peak, not average
blocks.content: Size your servers for average load and you will get paged the first time real traffic spikes. Every capacity number you compute should get multiplied by your peak factor before it decides a server count.

Some systems spike far past 3x, a viral post, a flash sale, a live sporting event. If the interviewer describes a spiky use case, say so out loud and bump your peak multiplier up, maybe 5x or 10x, and explain why you picked that number.
6. Storage Over Time, a Small Worked Example
blocks.text: 6. Storage Over Time, a Small Worked Example

blocks.content: Let us make this concrete with numbers small enough to do in your head. Say a system stores 1KB per record and creates 10 million records a day.
10,000,000 records times 1KB per record is 10,000,000 KB. Divide by 1,000 to get megabytes, that is 10,000 MB. Divide by 1,000 again to get gigabytes, that is 10GB a day.

Multiply 10GB a day by 365 days and you get roughly 3,650GB a year, call it 3.65TB. Say the whole chain out loud exactly like that, and the interviewer sees precisely how you think, not just the final number.

7. A Full Worked Example: A Twitter Like Service
blocks.text: 7. A Full Worked Example: A Twitter Like Service

blocks.content: Let us put every building block together on one system. Say we are designing a Twitter like service with 200 million daily active users.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383031-189783767.png
blocks.alt: DAU flowing through the fraction of users who post, into total tweets a day, into an average write QPS figure

blocks.content: First, writes. Assume half of active users post on a given day, so 200,000,000 x 0.5 gives 100,000,000 tweets a day.

Average write QPS: 100,000,000 divided by roughly 100,000 seconds gives about 1,000 tweets a second. Doing the fuller division by 86,400 gives closer to 1,160 a second, close enough either way to guide the design.
Peak write QPS at a 3x multiplier: roughly 3,000 to 3,500 tweets a second.

Now reads. Assume a 100 to 1 read to write ratio, since far more people scroll a timeline than post to it. Average read QPS: 1,160 x 100 is about 116,000 requests a second. Peak read QPS at 3x: around 350,000 a second.

Now storage. Say each tweet, text plus metadata, takes about 300 bytes. Daily text storage: 100,000,000 x 300 bytes is 30,000,000,000 bytes, which is 30GB a day. Over a year that comes to roughly 11TB.
Now media. Say 1 in every 10 tweets carries an image averaging 200KB. That is 10,000,000 images a day x 200KB, which is 2,000,000,000 KB, or 2TB a day. Over a year, roughly 730TB.
Finally bandwidth. Assume an average read payload of 2KB per request. 116,000 requests a second x 2KB is about 232,000 KB a second, roughly 227 MB a second, which lands close to 1.8 Gbps.

blocks.title: Every number here is an assumption
blocks.content: The half of users posting, the 100 to 1 read ratio, the 300 byte tweet, none of these are facts, they are reasonable starting assumptions stated out loud. Change any of them and the final numbers shift, which is exactly why saying the assumption matters more than the arithmetic.
8. The Interview Angle
None of this math is genuinely hard. The skill being tested is whether you can do it quickly, out loud, with reasonable assumptions, while someone is watching and the clock is running.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383031-502142582.png
blocks.alt: A candidate reasoning out loud, showing structured thinking, which raises the interviewer’s confidence before the design is even finished

blocks.content: Staying silent while you calculate in your head, or worse, refusing to guess because you do not have exact numbers, reads far worse than saying a rough number with a clearly stated assumption attached to it.
State your assumption, do the arithmetic in the open, round aggressively, and move on. That combination signals more competence in ninety seconds than a perfectly precise number ever will.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383031-446615190.png
blocks.alt: A capacity estimate built from four satellite building blocks, DAU, QPS, storage, and bandwidth

blocks.title: Recap
blocks.content: DAU feeds QPS. QPS splits into reads and writes. Item size times item count feeds storage. QPS times payload size feeds bandwidth. Multiply anything meant for capacity planning by your peak factor before you actually use it.
Get comfortable with this pattern and every interview that opens with design a system for this many users stops being scary. It is just five numbers, done out loud.
